author: Virginia Woolf
who: The narrator, in the first interlude
parts: The sun had not yet risen.
The sea was indistinguishable from the sky,
except that the sea was slightly creased
as if a cloth had wrinkles in it.
hints: An experimental English novel
Author's initials: V. W.
Six friends speak in turn from childhood to middle age, between interludes about the sea
note: The first words of Woolf's most experimental novel. Its italic interludes follow the sun across a single day while six voices cover whole lives.

author: Pearl S. Buck
hints: The bestselling novel in America that year
Author's initials: P. S. B.
A Chinese farmer, his wife O-lan, and the land
note: The opening of the novel that topped the US bestseller list in 1931 and 1932 and won the Pulitzer Prize. The Nobel Prize followed for Buck in 1938.

author: William Faulkner
parts: From beyond the screen of bushes
hints: A Southern novel its author called "a cheap idea"
Author's initials: W. F.
A Mississippi crime story: a gangster, a bootleggers' house, a kidnapped student
note: Faulkner later wrote that he conceived the book to make money. It became his first bestseller.

author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
parts: it is not meat nor drink
nor a roof against the rain;
hints: A sonnet from a sequence about a love affair
Author's initials: E. St. V. M.
The speaker lists everything love can't do, then admits she wouldn't trade it
note: Sonnet XXX of Fatal Interview, 52 sonnets about an affair that ends. It starts by denying love's power and ends by refusing to give it up.

author: Langston Hughes
parts: / To tell you a story of the long dark way
/ That I had to climb, that I had to know
/ In order that the race might live and grow.
hints: A poem written to be performed aloud
Author's initials: L. H.
A mother speaks to her children about the road from slavery
note: Hughes wrote it for his reading tour of the South and sold it as a cheap illustrated booklet, so audiences could take the poem home.

work: somewhere i have never travelled,gladly beyond
author: E. E. Cummings
hints: A love poem with almost no capital letters
Author's initials: E. E. C.
A beloved who opens the speaker the way spring opens a rose
note: From his 1931 collection ViVa. Its last line, about the rain's small hands, is one of the most quoted in American poetry.

author: Eugene O'Neill
who: Lavinia Mannon, to the servant Seth
parts: Living alone here with the dead
is a worse act of justice than death or prison!
hints: An American stage trilogy that retells a Greek tragedy
Author's initials: E. O'N.
A general comes home from the Civil War, and his wife and daughter go to war with each other
note: Lavinia's last speech. O'Neill moved Aeschylus's Oresteia to New England after the Civil War; at the end she shuts herself in the house with the family's dead.

author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
parts: It was a dark and stormy night,
when it was checked by a violent gust of wind
hints: A novel from the 1830s
Author's initials: E. B.-L.
A gentleman highwayman in London
note: The 1830 first edition, as here. The sentence goes on for another thirty words, which is why it became the byword for overwritten openings; a contest for the worst first line of a novel is named after its author.

author: Ford Madox Ford
hints: A novel from the 1910s
Author's initials: F. M. F.
Two married couples meet every year at a German spa, and the narrator notices nothing
note: He says "heard", but it is his own story: his wife's affair went on under his nose for nine years. The calm opening is the first sign we can't trust him.

author: J. M. Barrie
hints: A children's novel from the 1910s, based on the author's play
Author's initials: J. M. B.
A boy takes three London children to Neverland
note: The novel was first called Peter and Wendy. Six words give away the whole story, and the next sentence says the children all find out soon.

author: Miguel de Cervantes
parts: In a village of La Mancha,
the name of which I have no desire to call to mind,
there lived not long since one of those gentlemen
that keep a lance in the lance-rack, an old buckler,
a lean hack, and a greyhound for coursing.
hints: A Spanish novel from the 1600s, in translation
Author's initials: M. de C.
An old gentleman reads too many tales of chivalry and rides out as a knight
note: The lance, shield, thin horse and dog are a whole social class in a list: a gentleman with a name and no money. He is about to become a knight in his own mind.

author: Rafael Sabatini
hints: An adventure novel from the 1920s
Author's initials: R. S.
A young lawyer hides from the French Revolution in a troupe of travelling actors
note: The hero, André-Louis Moreau, lives up to it: a lawyer who becomes a clown, a fencing master and a revolutionary.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
parts: When Mary Lennox was sent to Misselthwaite Manor
the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen.
hints: A children's novel from the 1910s
Author's initials: F. H. B.
An orphan from India finds a locked garden on a Yorkshire estate
note: Burnett starts her heroine as unlikeable as possible, sour, sallow and rude, so the garden has something to mend.

author: E. M. Forster
parts: and they are twenty miles off—
hints: A novel from the 1920s
Author's initials: E. M. F.
An Englishwoman visits caves in British India, and an Indian doctor is accused
note: The first sentence sets aside the one thing that matters. What happens, or doesn't, in the caves is the centre of the book, and Forster never says.

author: Horace Walpole
parts: than any casque ever made for human being,
and shaded with a proportionable quantity of black feathers.
hints: The first novel to call itself Gothic
Author's initials: H. W.
On his wedding day a prince's son is crushed by something that falls from the sky
note: The story begins when this giant helmet falls into the courtyard and kills the bridegroom. Walpole first passed the book off as a translation of an old Italian manuscript.

author: John Keats
parts: O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms,
/ The sedge has wither'd from the lake,
hints: A ballad from the 1810s
Author's initials: J. K.
A knight meets a beautiful lady in the meadows and wakes alone on a cold hillside
note: Keats copied it into a letter in April 1819. The printed version of 1820 changed the knight to a "wretched wight"; most readers know the letter's version.

author: Jane Austen
parts: No one who had ever seen Catherine Morland in her infancy
hints: A novel from the 1810s that teases the Gothic craze
Author's initials: J. A.
A young reader of horror novels visits a real abbey and imagines a crime
note: Austen's send-up of the novels everyone was reading. Catherine is ordinary on purpose, and the abbey's dark secret turns out to be a laundry list.

author: J. Sheridan Le Fanu
parts: I live in your warm life,
hints: A novella from the 1870s
Author's initials: J. S. Le F.
A lonely girl in an Austrian castle befriends a guest who sleeps all day
note: A vampire story twenty-five years before Dracula, and it says out loud what Dracula only hints at: Carmilla's hunger is also love.

author: Edgar Allan Poe
parts: very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am;
hints: A short story from the 1840s
Author's initials: E. A. P.
A murderer insists he is sane, but hears his victim's heart beating under the floor
note: The narrator argues for his sanity in the first sentence, and the rest of the story is his proof, which proves the opposite.

author: Henry James
who: The narrator of the frame story
parts: but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome,
hints: A novella from the 1890s
Author's initials: H. J.
A governess believes two ghosts want the children in her care
note: The book opens with people telling ghost stories on Christmas Eve, and the story we get is a manuscript read aloud. James keeps us at a distance from the start, so we never know whether to believe the governess.

author: Wilkie Collins
parts: of what a Woman's patience can endure,
hints: A sensation novel from the 1860s
Author's initials: W. C.
A drawing teacher meets a ghostly figure on a moonlit road outside London
note: Collins tells the story through several witnesses, like evidence at a trial. It first ran weekly in Dickens's magazine All the Year Round.

author: William Shakespeare
parts: For aught that I could ever read,
/ Could ever hear by tale or history,
hints: A comedy from the 1590s
Spoken by a young man whose love has just been forbidden to marry him
Four lovers lost in a wood near Athens, fairies, and a weaver with a donkey's head
note: Lysander says it to comfort Hermia, whose father wants her married to someone else. The rest of the play proves him right, with fairies making it worse.

author: William Shakespeare
who: Portia, disguised as a lawyer, to Shylock
parts: / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
hints: A comedy from the 1590s
Spoken by a woman disguised as a young lawyer
A loan secured by a pound of flesh, and a trial in Venice
note: "Strained" means forced: mercy can't be compelled. Portia asks Shylock to be merciful, he refuses, and she beats him on a technicality instead.

author: William Shakespeare
hints: A history play from the 1590s
The play's first line, spoken by a duke who will murder his way to the crown
Two princes in the Tower, and a horse he'd trade his kingdom for
note: Often quoted as if the winter is now. It isn't: the winter has been turned into summer by the new king, Richard's brother, the "sun" of York. Richard is bored by peace.

author: William Shakespeare
hints: A history play from 1599
A king rallies his soldiers at a siege in France
A young English king, once a wild prince, wins at Agincourt
note: The siege of Harfleur. The breach is a gap blown in the town wall; if they can't get through it, Henry says, they should fill it with their bodies.

author: William Shakespeare
parts: my dog bark at a crow
hints: A comedy from the 1590s
Spoken by a woman who trades insults with a soldier
Two sworn enemies of marriage are tricked into falling in love in Messina
note: Beatrice says it in the first scene, to Benedick. By the end of the play he swears exactly that, and she believes him.

author: William Shakespeare
hints: A tragedy from the 1600s
Spoken by a blunt soldier describing a queen
A Roman general gives up half an empire for an Egyptian queen
note: Enobarbus is the play's cynic, so the praise counts. He is explaining why Antony will never leave her, just after Antony has agreed to marry someone else.

author: William Shakespeare
hints: A late play, half tragedy and half comedy
Not a line of speech at all
A jealous king, an abandoned baby, and a statue that comes to life
note: The most famous stage direction in English. Antigonus has just left the baby Perdita on a shore; the bear eats him, and the play turns from tragedy to comedy.

author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
parts: / I love thee to the depth and breadth and height
hints: A sonnet from the 1850s, number 43 of a sequence
Author's initials: E. B. B.
Love sonnets written during a secret courtship with another poet
note: She wrote the sequence while Robert Browning was courting her against her father's wishes. They married in secret and left for Italy.

author: William Shakespeare
parts: Let me not to the marriage of true minds
/ Which alters when it alteration finds,
hints: A sonnet from 1609
Author's initials: W. S.
Often read at weddings: real love doesn't change when circumstances do
note: "Impediments" echoes the marriage service, where the priest asks whether anyone knows a reason the couple may not marry.

author: Robert Burns
parts: O my Luve's like a red, red rose,
/ O my Luve's like the melodie,
hints: A song from the 1790s
Author's initials: R. B.
A Scottish lover promises to love till the seas run dry
note: Burns collected and reworked old Scots songs, and this one stitches together lines from earlier ballads. Bob Dylan has called it his greatest inspiration.

author: Lord Byron
parts: She walks in beauty, like the night
/ Of cloudless climes and starry skies;
/ And all that's best of dark and bright
/ Meet in her aspect and her eyes:
hints: A poem from the 1810s
Author's initials: Lord B.
A poet sees a woman in a black mourning dress at a party
note: Byron is said to have written it after seeing his cousin by marriage in mourning, black dress with spangles. The beauty is in the mix of dark and light.

work: The Passionate Shepherd to His Love
author: Christopher Marlowe
parts: / And we will all the pleasures prove
/ That hills and valleys, dales and fields,
hints: A poem from the 1590s
Author's initials: C. M.
A shepherd promises his love beds of roses and a gown of the finest wool
note: This is the text of England's Helicon (1600), as in the Oxford Book of English Verse. Walter Raleigh wrote the nymph's reply: flowers fade, wool wears out, and shepherds lie.

author: Emily Dickinson
hints: A short poem first printed in the 1890s, after its author's death
Author's initials: E. D.
A speaker longs to be moored for the night in a lover's harbour
note: Her first editor, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, worried that readers would read too much into it. He printed it anyway.

author: Edmond Rostand
who: Cyrano, to Roxane (Gladys Thomas and Mary F. Guillemard's 1898 translation)
parts: A kiss, when all is said,—what is it?
/ An oath that's ratified,—a sealed promise,
hints: A French verse play from the 1890s, in translation
Author's initials: E. R.
A swordsman with an enormous nose writes love letters for a handsome friend
note: Cyrano says it in the dark under Roxane's balcony, speaking for his handsome friend Christian, who then climbs up to get the kiss. In Rostand's French the dot goes on the i of "aimer".

author: Homer
who: The poet, calling on the Muse (Samuel Butler's 1898 translation)
parts: the anger of Achilles son of Peleus,
hints: An epic from ancient Greek, translated by Samuel Butler
Author: traditionally called H.
Ten years into a war, a quarrel over a captive woman splits the Greek camp at Troy
note: The poem's first subject is a feeling, not a war. Butler, who also translated the Odyssey (day 22), turned Homer into plain prose.

author: Dante Alighieri
parts: Midway upon the journey of our life
/ I found myself within a forest dark,
hints: A poem from 1300s Italy, translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
Author's initials: D. A.
A poet lost in a wood is led down through the circles of Hell
note: Dante was 35, halfway through the Bible's three score and ten. Longfellow kept the line count of the Italian exactly, and gave up rhyme to do it.

author: Gustave Flaubert
parts: human speech is like a cracked tin kettle,
on which we hammer out tunes
when we long to move the stars.
hints: A French novel from the 1850s, translated by Eleanor Marx-Aveling
Author's initials: G. F.
A doctor's wife in Normandy, bored by her marriage, ruins herself for romance
note: Flaubert spent days on single sentences, and here he admits language can never be good enough. His translator was Karl Marx's youngest daughter.

author: Victor Hugo
who: The Bishop, to Jean Valjean (Isabel F. Hapgood's 1887 translation)
parts: you no longer belong to evil,
It is your soul that I buy from you;
hints: A French novel from the 1860s, translated by Isabel F. Hapgood
Author's initials: V. H.
A released convict steals a bishop's silver, and the bishop lets him keep it
note: The police have brought Valjean back with the stolen silver. The bishop says it was a gift, adds two candlesticks, and changes Valjean's life.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
parts: On an exceptionally hot evening early in July
a young man came out of the garret
in which he lodged in S. Place
and walked slowly, as though in hesitation, towards K. bridge.
hints: A Russian novel from the 1860s, translated by Constance Garnett
Author's initials: F. D.
A poor student in St Petersburg kills a pawnbroker to test a theory
note: Raskolnikov is rehearsing the murder on this walk. Garnett, who also translated Anna Karenina (day 17), brought most of the Russian classics into English.

author: Henrik Ibsen
who: Nora, to Helmer (R. Farquharson Sharp's 1910 translation)
parts: just as at home I was papa's doll-child;
hints: A Norwegian play from the 1870s, translated by R. Farquharson Sharp
Author's initials: H. I.
A wife with a secret debt finally sees her marriage clearly
note: Nora is about to walk out on her husband and children. For a German production the leading actress refused to play that ending, and Ibsen, under protest, wrote one where she stays.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
hints: A German verse play from 1808, translated by Bayard Taylor
Author's initials: J. W. von G.
A scholar bored with all knowledge makes a wager with the devil
note: Faust says it on an Easter walk, before he meets the devil: one soul clings to the world, the other wants to fly. Taylor kept Goethe's metres and rhymes.

author: Ernest Hemingway
who: Jake Barnes, the narrator, answering Brett
parts: The car slowed suddenly pressing Brett against me.
hints: A novel from the 1920s
Author's initials: E. H.
American and British expatriates drink their way from Paris to the bullfights in Pamplona
note: Brett has just said they could have had "such a damned good time together". A policeman's raised baton cuts in before Jake answers. He was wounded in the war and can't be her lover.

author: James Joyce
parts: as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe
like the descent of their last end,
upon all the living and the dead.
hints: The last story in a collection from the 1910s
Author's initials: J. J.
After a Christmas party in Dublin, a man learns his wife once loved a boy who died
note: The last sentence of Dubliners. "Falling faintly ... faintly falling" turns back on itself, like the snow settling on everything.

author: Charles Dickens
parts: and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light
hints: A novel from the 1860s
Author's initials: C. D.
A blacksmith's boy is made a gentleman by a secret benefactor
note: Dickens first wrote a sadder ending. Bulwer-Lytton (day 68) persuaded him to change it, and even this happier one is careful not to promise.

author: D. H. Lawrence
parts: He would not take that direction,
to the darkness, to follow her.
He walked towards the faintly humming, glowing town,
hints: A novel from the 1910s
Author's initials: D. H. L.
A miner's son in Nottinghamshire is torn between his mother and the women he loves
note: "Her" is his mother, who has just died. Paul has thought about following her; the last word is his choice to live.

author: Jonathan Swift
parts: that they will not presume to come in my sight.
hints: A satire from the 1720s
Author's initials: J. S.
A ship's surgeon visits tiny people, giants, a flying island and a land of horses
note: The vice is pride. Gulliver comes home from the land of the wise horses unable to stand other people, his own family included.

work: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
author: Robert Frost
parts: The woods are lovely, dark and deep,
/ But I have promises to keep,
/ And miles to go before I sleep,
/ And miles to go before I sleep.
hints: A poem from the 1920s
Author's initials: R. F.
A rider stops his horse by a wood on the darkest evening of the year
note: The last line repeats the one before it, and the repeat changes it: the second time, "sleep" sounds like more than a night's rest.

author: T. S. Eliot
parts: This is the way the world ends
hints: A poem from the 1920s
Author's initials: T. S. E.
Empty men, stuffed with straw, chant in a dead land
note: The poem ends on a children's rhyme, "Here we go round the mulberry bush", bent out of shape. "This is the way the world ends" is said three times before the last line.

author: Virginia Woolf
parts: and a room of her own
hints: A long essay from the 1920s, first given as lectures
Author's initials: V. W.
Asked to talk about women and fiction, a writer invents Shakespeare's gifted sister
note: Woolf said it in lectures at Cambridge women's colleges in 1928. The money she has in mind is five hundred pounds a year, and the room has a lock.

work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
hints: A treatise from the 1790s
Author's initials: M. W.
A reply to those who would educate girls only to please men
note: Wollstonecraft's daughter was Mary Shelley, who wrote Frankenstein (day 5). She argues that education, not nature, makes women seem weaker.

search.title: vindication of the rights of woman
search.creator: wollstonecraft

author: Emily Dickinson
parts: / Then there's a pair of us—don't tell!
hints: A poem first printed in the 1890s
Author's initials: E. D.
Two secret nobodies agree that being somebody would be dreary
note: Almost none of Dickinson's nearly 1,800 poems were printed while she lived. This is the first printed text, of 1891; the standard modern edition, made from her manuscript, reads "they'd advertise".

work: How It Feels to Be Colored Me
author: Zora Neale Hurston
hints: A magazine essay from the 1920s
Author's initials: Z. N. H.
A writer remembers the day she "became colored", when she left her Florida town at thirteen
note: Hurston grew up in Eatonville, an all-Black town in Florida. The essay refuses the pity readers expected from her.

author: Willa Cather
parts: there are only two or three human stories,
and they go on repeating themselves
as fiercely as if they had never happened before;
like the larks in this country,
hints: A novel from the 1910s
Author's initials: W. C.
A Swedish immigrant's daughter makes the Nebraska prairie pay
note: The larks have been singing the same five notes for thousands of years. Cather took her title from a Whitman poem.

author: Edith Wharton
parts: In the afternoon rush of the Grand Central Station
by the sight of Miss Lily Bart.
hints: A novel from the 1900s
Author's initials: E. W.
A beautiful, penniless woman in New York society runs out of time to marry well
note: We meet Lily through a man's eyes, as society will judge her all book long. The title comes from Ecclesiastes: "the heart of fools is in the house of mirth."

author: Elizabeth Gaskell
parts: Cranford is in possession of the Amazons;
all the holders of houses above a certain rent
hints: A novel from the 1850s, first a magazine serial
Author's initials: E. G.
Genteel widows and spinsters in a small English town keep up appearances
note: Gaskell's sketches first ran in Dickens's magazine Household Words. Men in Cranford, the narrator says, are "so in the way".

author: Daniel Defoe
parts: It happened one day, about noon, going towards my boat,
with the print of a man's naked foot on the shore,
which was very plain to be seen on the sand.
hints: A novel from the 1710s
Author's initials: D. D.
A castaway spends twenty-eight years on an island
note: Crusoe has been alone for fifteen years. One footprint terrifies him more than the shipwreck did.

author: King James Version
parts: To every thing there is a season,
and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
hints: A book of wisdom, in an English translation of 1611
Traditionally credited to a king, the son of David
A preacher says all is vanity, then lists a time for everything
note: Ecclesiastes 3:1–2. Pete Seeger set these verses to music as "Turn! Turn! Turn!", a number-one hit for the Byrds in 1965.

search.title: bible
search.q: title:(holy bible) AND (king james OR authorized version) AND mediatype:texts

author: W. B. Yeats
parts: I will arise and go now,
/ And a small cabin build there,
hints: A poem from the 1890s
Author's initials: W. B. Y.
On a grey London pavement a man dreams of an island with bean rows and a beehive
note: Yeats said a fountain in a London shop window, with a little ball balanced on its jet, set off the memory of a lake in Sligo.

author: Oscar Wilde
hints: A comedy from the 1890s
Author's initials: O. W.
A young wife suspects her husband, and a woman with a past saves her reputation
note: Wilde gives his most hopeful line to a seducer, late at night, among men trading cynical jokes.

author: Arthur Conan Doyle
hints: A detective novel from the 1900s
Author's initials: A. C. D.
A family curse on the moors of Devon
note: The end of chapter two, written for a magazine serial. Mortimer found the prints beside the dead body of Sir Charles Baskerville.

author: Langston Hughes
parts: / I've known rivers ancient as the world
and older than the flow of human blood in human veins.
/ My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
hints: A poem from the 1920s
Author's initials: L. H.
A speaker remembers the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi
note: Hughes wrote it at about 18 on a train crossing the Mississippi. It was printed in The Crisis in June 1921.

author: Henry David Thoreau
parts: because I wished to live deliberately,
to front only the essential facts of life,
and see if I could not learn what it had to teach,
and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
hints: A book from the 1850s
Author's initials: H. D. T.
A man builds a cabin by a pond in Massachusetts and lives there two years
note: The woods were a mile from his neighbours and two from Concord, on land owned by Emerson. He walked into town most days.

author: A. A. Milne
parts: coming downstairs now, bump, bump, bump,
on the back of his head,
hints: A children's book from the 1920s
Author's initials: A. A. M.
A bear of very little brain lives in the Hundred Acre Wood
note: The book's first sentence. He is still Edward Bear, the name of Christopher Milne's real teddy; the Winnie came from a black bear at London Zoo.

author: L. Frank Baum
parts: No matter how dreary and gray our homes are,
we people of flesh and blood would rather live there than in any other country,
There is no place like home.
hints: A children's novel from 1900
Author's initials: L. F. B.
A Kansas girl, a cyclone, and three companions on a yellow brick road
note: The Scarecrow can't see why anyone would leave Oz for grey Kansas. The ruby slippers came with the 1939 film; in the book they are silver shoes.

author: Margery Williams
who: The Skin Horse, to the Rabbit
parts: “It's a thing that happens to you.
When a child loves you for a long, long time, not just to play with, but REALLY loves you, then you become Real.”
hints: A children's book from the 1920s
Author's initials: M. W.
A stuffed toy rabbit learns from an old toy horse how toys come alive
note: The Skin Horse is the oldest toy in the nursery, and his seams show. He warns the Rabbit that becoming Real can hurt.

author: Rudyard Kipling
parts: In the High and Far-Off Times
hints: A book of animal stories for children from the 1900s
Author's initials: R. K.
How the leopard got his spots and the camel his hump
note: From "The Elephant's Child". Kipling first told the stories to his daughter Josephine, the Best Beloved; she died at six, three years before the book came out.

author: Edward Lear
parts: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat went to sea
/ They took some honey, and plenty of money
/ Wrapped up in a five-pound note.
hints: A nonsense poem from the 1870s
Author's initials: E. L.
Two animals elope, buy a ring from a pig, and dance by the light of the moon
note: Lear wrote it for a friend's small daughter who was ill. The "runcible spoon" in the last verse is a word he made up.

author: Lewis Carroll
parts: (she was so much surprised, that for the moment
she quite forgot how to speak good English);
hints: A children's book from the 1860s
Author's initials: L. C.
A girl follows a white rabbit down a hole
note: She has just eaten a cake and grown nine feet tall. Carroll (day 38 was Through the Looking-Glass) makes the grammar mistake part of the joke.

author: Kenneth Grahame
parts: had been working very hard all the morning,
hints: A children's novel from the 1900s
Author's initials: K. G.
A mole, a water rat, a badger and a reckless toad by an English river
note: A few lines later the Mole says "Hang spring-cleaning!" and leaves the work. Grahame began the stories as bedtime tales for his son.

author: Alexander Pope
hints: A poem from the 1710s, written when its author was in his early twenties
Author's initials: A. P.
Rules for critics, in rhyming couplets
note: The same poem gives us "a little learning is a dang'rous thing" and "fools rush in where angels fear to tread".

author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
parts: / Where Alph, the sacred river, ran
hints: A poem from the 1810s
Author's initials: S. T. C.
A vision of an emperor's palace, cut short by a visitor from Porlock
note: Coleridge said the poem came to him in an opium dream, and that a visitor "on business from Porlock" broke it off. He published it as a fragment.

work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
parts: how a man was made a slave;
how a slave was made a man.
hints: A memoir from the 1840s
Author's initials: F. D.
A man born enslaved in Maryland teaches himself to read, fights back, and escapes north
note: Douglass writes this just before telling how he fought the "slave-breaker" Edward Covey, the turning point of his life. He published the book at about 27, at the risk of being recaptured.

author: H. G. Wells
parts: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century
that this world was being watched keenly and closely
and yet as mortal as his own;
hints: A novel from the 1890s
Author's initials: H. G. W.
Cylinders land near Woking, and tripods walk out
note: "As mortal as his own" gives away the ending in the first sentence: the invaders die of ordinary germs.

author: L. M. Montgomery
parts: that to-morrow is a new day
hints: A novel from the 1900s
Author's initials: L. M. M.
An orphan girl with red hair is sent by mistake to a brother and sister on Prince Edward Island
note: Anne says it after a day of disasters. Montgomery built the book from a note she had made years earlier: a couple ask for a boy and are sent a girl. ("To-morrow" is the 1908 first edition's spelling.)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
parts: adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines.
hints: An essay from the 1840s
Author's initials: R. W. E.
An American argues: trust yourself, not society
note: Usually quoted without "foolish", which changes it. Emerson's point is that you may contradict yesterday's self if today's is right.

author: Christopher Marlowe
parts: / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium—
/ Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss.—
hints: A play from the 1590s
Author's initials: C. M.
A scholar sells his soul to the devil for twenty-four years of power
note: From the 1604 printing (the A-text); the dash after "kiss" leads into the kiss itself. Helen is a spirit the devil has conjured, so the kiss damns him. Goethe's Faust (day 102) retells the same legend two centuries later.

alias: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
author: Anonymous
parts: and went to the door concealed among the bushes,
hints: A tale from a Middle Eastern story collection, retold in English by Andrew Lang
Told by a queen, night after night, to stay alive
A woodcutter spies on forty robbers and their secret cave
note: Ali Baba is in no Arabic manuscript of the Nights. Antoine Galland added it to his French version in the 1700s, from a story told him by the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab.

author: Omar Khayyám
parts: nor all thy Piety nor Wit / Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line,
/ Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it.
hints: Persian verses of the 1100s, in Edward FitzGerald's free English version
Author's initials: O. K.
A poet urges wine and the present moment, because what's done can't be undone
note: This game takes its name from this verse. FitzGerald's version sold almost nothing at first, until Rossetti and Swinburne found copies marked down to a penny.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
who: The poet (his own translation from Bengali)
parts: Where the mind is without fear
and the head is held high;
/ Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls;
hints: Song offerings from 1912, translated from Bengali by their author
Author's initials: R. T.
A poet prays that his country will wake into a heaven of freedom
note: Poem 35. Tagore made the English versions himself, and the next year became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

author: Confucius
who: The Master, to Tsze-kung (James Legge's 1861 translation)
parts: Is not RECIPROCITY such a word?
hints: Sayings of a Chinese teacher from about 500 BCE, translated by James Legge
Author: known in English as C.
A student asks for one word that can guide a whole life
note: The Golden Rule turned around, five centuries before the Gospels. Legge was a Scottish missionary who became Oxford's first professor of Chinese.

author: Li Bai
who: The wife, to her husband (Ezra Pound's 1915 version)
parts: While my hair was still cut straight across my forehead
/ I played about the front gate, pulling flowers.
/ You came by on bamboo stilts,
hints: A Chinese poem of the 700s, in Ezra Pound's English version
The poet, as Pound named him: R.
A young wife writes to her husband, away on a long trading journey
note: Pound read no Chinese. He worked from the notes of the scholar Ernest Fenollosa and called the poet by his Japanese name, Rihaku.

author: Aesop
parts: The Tortoise never for a moment stopped,
but went on with a slow but steady pace
hints: Greek fables from about 2,500 years ago, translated by George Fyler Townsend
Author's initial: A.
A boastful animal takes a nap halfway through a race
note: Moments later the Hare wakes and runs, too late. The moral everyone knows, "slow and steady wins the race", isn't in Townsend's printed text: he lets the story make the point.

author: Hans Christian Andersen
hints: A Danish fairy tale from the 1830s, translated by Mary Howitt
Author's initials: H. C. A.
Two swindlers sell a vain ruler cloth that only the clever can see
note: Everyone else has pretended to see the cloth so as not to look stupid. The child's line breaks the spell, and the Emperor keeps walking anyway.

Authors: two brothers, J. and W. G.
A girl locked in a tower with no door or stairs
note: A prince overhears the call and uses it himself. In the Grimms' first edition Rapunzel gives the visits away by asking why her clothes have grown so tight.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
hints: A book of essays from 1903
Author's initials: W. E. B. D.
A sociologist describes "double-consciousness": seeing yourself through the eyes of others
note: Du Bois says it first in the book's Forethought and again here, in chapter two. His idea of "double-consciousness" is still taught a century later.

work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

/ Which is the bliss of solitude,

hints: A poem from the 1800s
Author's initials: W. W.
A walker by a lake comes on a crowd of golden flowers
note: The walk was with his sister Dorothy, in April 1802. Her journal describes the daffodils first; the two best lines of the poem are said to be by his wife, Mary.

author: Herman Melville
who: The lawyer, the narrator, then Bartleby

Author's initials: H. M.
A Wall Street lawyer hires a copyist who gradually stops doing anything
note: The first time Bartleby says it. He goes on saying it to every request until he dies, and the narrator never finds out why.

Author's initials: T. S. E.
A timid man on his way to a tea party wonders whether he dares to eat a peach
note: Eliot was in his early twenties when he wrote it, about a man who feels middle-aged. Ezra Pound got it printed in Poetry magazine.

work: The Charge of the Light Brigade

hints: A poem from the 1850s

British cavalry ride into Russian guns after a blundered order

author: Robert Herrick

hints: A poem from the 1640s
Author's initials: R. H.
A poet tells young women to marry while they can
